preamble.text: Historical snapshot: later evidence may be reflected in current research pages and corrections.
Deterministically compiled from canonical evidence. Importance measures impact, not truth; evidence/confidence remain separate.

blocks.text: 1. A mathematical-analysis preprint reports mismatches between OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof and cited Lean estimates

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported mismatches hold, a machine-checked Lean result cannot be treated as verification of the specific natural-language proof without a semantic bridge. This changes how an extraordinary mathematical claim should be evaluated, although the audit does not refute the underlying theorem.

What changed: Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen compare OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes proof with cited Lean declarations. For Lemma 8.6, equation (8.19), they report that the manuscript states an m+4 derivative estimate while the cited Lean estimate requires m+5. For pressure-flux equation (10.19), they report a different Lean bound and proof route, including an additional localized gradient norm. Static inspection of the pinned source shows a related canonical cutoff-flux bound is used along the option-C proof path; whether it is equivalent or sufficient for the manuscript argument remains unresolved. The authors do not claim the natural-language blow-up proof is incorrect. The critique remains an author-reported result without independent reproduction or established specialist consensus. Why it matters: A formal proof establishes its encoded theorem, but it does not by itself establish that the theorem matches the natural-language argument it is meant to check. The reported estimate differences give concrete targets for independent Lean and PDE review of an extraordinary mathematical claim, while leaving the truth of the underlying blow-up result unresolved.

Claimed: The authors report an m+4 versus m+5 derivative requirement in Lemma 8.6 and a distinct pressure-flux estimate/proof route for equation (10.19), challenging correspondence between selected manuscript arguments and cited Lean declarations.

Mechanism: Compares selected estimates and proof steps in OpenAI’s natural-language Navier–Stokes paper against cited Lean declarations and pinned source revisions. The critique separates encoded theorem validity from semantic fidelity to the written argument.

Strongest baseline: OpenAI’s natural-language paper and its cited Lean declarations are compared directly. The authors report explicit estimate differences but do not claim the natural-language theorem is false; neither the critique nor theorem has independent peer-reviewed resolution in this review.

Regime: Selected analytic estimates in one natural-language Navier–Stokes proof and corresponding Lean declarations at pinned revision f9e8bc5; static inspection traces a related cutoff-flux bound to option C but does not settle semantic fidelity or theorem correctness.

Limitations: This is an author-reported analysis in an arXiv v1 preprint; peer review and independent specialist consensus were not established.; The paper compares selected proof components and cited Lean declarations; it does not establish that the underlying Navier–Stokes blow-up theorem is false.; For pressure-flux equation (10.19), the authors report a different bound involving localized gradient norm A_R. Static inspection places a related canonical cutoff-flux bound on the option-C proof path, but does not show that the two arguments are equivalent or that the Lean inequality is insufficient.; No independent reproduction, Lean build, proof of estimate equivalence, or audit of later upstream revisions was performed.

Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of the reported m+4/m+5 or pressure-flux estimate comparisons, proof of equivalence between the code-path cutoff-flux bound and manuscript equation (10.19), or reconciliation against later OpenAI repository revisions has been completed.; The critique does not refute the underlying blow-up theorem. Static inspection traces a related canonical cutoff-flux bound into the option-C proof path, but whether that bound is sufficient or semantically equivalent to manuscript equation (10.19) remains unresolved; the derivative-order mismatch and complete theorem-level implications also need expert assessment.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.08144v1 · https://github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler/tree/f9e8bc5b38b6e212696e8a30e3e91517af887bbd
2. Australia sets a national foundation for AI assurance across government

Desk: policy_geopolitics Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If adopted across Australian, state and territory governments, a common assurance foundation could shape AI development, procurement and deployment in public services at national scale. The framework leaves detailed policy to jurisdictions, and the publication provides no adoption or outcome evidence.

What changed: Australia’s national framework for assurance of AI use in government was agreed and released by the Data and Digital Ministers Meeting on 21 June 2024. It sets a shared foundation for Australian, state and territory governments across development, procurement and deployment, while leaving detailed policy to each jurisdiction. A 22 October 2026 ministerial statement reiterates support for safe and responsible government AI and describes the framework as a key step; it does not announce a new framework or establish binding adoption or measured outcomes. Why it matters: A shared assurance foundation can shape how governments assess AI development, procurement and deployment. The framework dates to June 2024 and leaves detailed policy to each jurisdiction; the October 2026 statement does not establish implementation, binding force or measured outcomes.
Demonstrated: Official Department of Finance pages establish that the framework was agreed and released on 21 June 2024 and document its scope, assurance cornerstones and mapped practices.
Claimed: The framework is intended to provide a nationally consistent foundation and support safe, responsible government AI use.
Mechanism: A national framework maps Australia’s AI Ethics Principles to governance and risk-based, lifecycle assurance practices for government AI development, procurement and deployment.

Strongest baseline: Earlier jurisdictional government AI guidance and the 2019 Australian AI Ethics Principles; the 21 June 2024 national framework adds a shared assurance foundation while preserving local policy development. A 22 October 2026 ministerial statement reaffirms safe/responsible use but does not establish a new policy event.
Regime: Australian, state and territory government AI use; policies are to be developed within jurisdictional legal and operational contexts.

Limitations: The framework is foundational and leaves detailed policies and guidance to each jurisdiction’s legislative, policy and operational context.; No binding force, common adoption deadline or jurisdictional implementation status is established by the pages reviewed.; No measured safety, reliability or public-service outcome is reported.; A NSW state strategy says agencies will comply with the NSW AI Assurance Framework; this is one jurisdiction-specific commitment and does not establish implementation across Australia.; The official framework landing page states that it was agreed and released on 21 June 2024; the pages dated October 2026 do not establish a new framework release. The 22 October 2026 ministers’ statement reiterates support and describes the existing framework as a key step.

Open evidence gaps: Jurisdiction-specific implementation policies, binding status and adoption dates were not enumerated.; The framework reports intended assurance practices, not measured implementation or outcomes.

Sources: https://www.finance.gov.au/government/public-data/data-and-digital-ministers-meeting/national-framework-assurance-artificial-intelligence-government/introduction · https://www.finance.gov.au/government/public-data/data-and-digital-ministers-meeting/national-framework-assurance-artificial-intelligence-government/cornerstones-assurance · https://www.finance.gov.au/government/public-data/data-and-digital-ministers-meeting/national-framework-assurance-artificial-intelligence-government/implementing-australias-ai-ethics-principles-government · https://www.digital.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-01/2026-2028-NSW-Government-Cyber-Security-Strategy.pdf · https://www.finance.gov.au/government/public-data/data-and-digital-ministers-meeting/national-framework-assurance-artificial-intelligence-government · https://www.finance.gov.au/government/public-data/data-and-digital-ministers-meeting/national-framework-assurance-artificial-intelligence-government/statement-data-and-digital-ministers

For Lemma 8.6, equation (8.19), they report that the manuscript states an m+4 derivative estimate while the cited Lean estimate requires m+5. For pressure-flux equation (10.19), they report a different Lean bound and proof route, including an additional localized gradient norm. Static inspection of the pinned source shows a related canonical cutoff-flux bound is used along the option-C proof path; whether it is equivalent or sufficient for the manuscript argument remains unresolved. The authors do not claim the natural-language blow-up proof is incorrect. The critique remains an author-reported result without independent reproduction or established specialist consensus. — FCMO-2DD7299410CB

EpiSEM-Bench tests evidence-dependent safety and useful recovery in tool agents — importance 5/10 · The authors introduce EpiSEM-Bench, with 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs over six tool-use domains, fact-level omission of safety evidence and an optional recovery tool. In one reported evaluation of ten models, access to recovery reduced unsafe execution on matched conditions for every model; nine also improved permissible-task completion, while one declined slightly. These are author-reported synthetic-benchmark findings, not independent or live-system results. — FCMO-43B701C7F278

Google DeepMind preprint extends Boyd-family records across high polynomial degrees — importance 5/10 · A Google DeepMind preprint presents a five-parameter extension of Boyd's construction for small Mahler-measure polynomials. The authors report verified irreducible examples below Boyd's limit point at all 995 even degrees they evaluate from 12 to 2000, including six improvements over published values. This advances finite-degree records but does not settle Lehmer's conjecture or prove every listed polynomial globally minimal; the reported results have not been independently reproduced in this review. — FCMO-D3D50BB885F2

Sensorimotor alignment correlates with embodied-model success in limited cohorts — importance 4/10 · A new preprint introduces Sensorimotor Alignment (S²), a training-free offline metric comparing a model’s sensory-feature neighborhoods with recorded robot-motion neighborhoods. The authors report that S² correlates with task success across 12 vision-language-action models (Pearson r=0.717; model-bootstrap 95% CI 0.436–0.912), as well as smaller VLM and world-action-model cohorts. The result suggests a possible low-cost screening signal before closed-loop evaluation, but it is correlational, tested on few model families, and does not show that optimizing S² improves success. The authors’ code guide also says their highlighted real-robot correlation uses an exploratory horizon; at the paper-prespecified horizon it is weaker. — FCMO-5ABCEA930CA1

Controlled tests show decision-model reliability depends on rule conflict, wording, and supplied information — importance 4/10 · A 2026-10-21 arXiv paper proposes controlled tests of decision models using executable arithmetic rules, crossed rule/state cases, equivalent wording changes and manipulated value tables. The authors report that transfer gains depend on agreement with source examples; under fully conflicting rule quartets, results differ in sign across two source splits and joint correctness is low. In tests of TypeSafe's Jev service, answers change more across equivalent wordings than across identical-text repeats and often follow altered table values or mappings. These are author-reported results on synthetic finite-domain tasks and one service version; code and data are stated as forthcoming, and this activation did not independently reproduce the analyses. — FCMO-85DE30B70CE3

items: MoEZip reports stronger task scores under aggressive KV-cache compression in tested sparse language models — importance 4/10 · An arXiv paper proposes MoEZip, which uses router Fisher-trace sensitivity and attention to retain context positions intended to stabilize expert routing during KV-cache eviction. In author-run comparisons, it reports higher long-context benchmark scores than KVZip, SnapKV and PyramidKV at high compression on Qwen3 and GLM-4.7-Flash sparse models. In a Qwen3-235B-A22B appendix, the authors report a 10-task LongBench macro of 44.7 versus 27.6 for KVZip at 10% KV retention. The authors also estimate 15,000–16,000 A100 GPU-hours for MoEZip and all baselines together, excluding preliminary or failed runs. The exact paper title also appears in NeurIPS 2026’s official downloads listing; this confirms conference-program inclusion but does not independently reproduce the benchmark results. The reported results have not been independently reproduced; Appendix C says code is in supplementary material, which this activation did not retrieve, while the linked repository page lists only a README and license. — FCMO-09C2A1F31683

items: Anthropic announces transfer of Agent Skills stewardship to the Agentic AI Foundation — importance 5/10 · Anthropic announced that it is donating the Agent Skills name and logo, GitHub organization and agentskills.io domain to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), which it describes as a neutral home for the standard. It says engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, and proposes a roadmap for versioned releases, formal proposals and security guidance. These are statements in Anthropic’s announcement; the proposed processes and governance outcomes are not yet demonstrated. Anthropic also reports adoption figures that have not been independently verified. — FCMO-87E21BE22609
